idiom_name: Diesel table! module (orders::table + QueryDsl) over Vec<Row>
implementation_notes: Diesel generates the pattern literally: table! declares a module per table containing a table struct, per-column types and a typed query DSL, and load() materializes the record set as Vec<YourRow>; the module's rules are ordinary functions taking &mut Connection and returning those vectors. The generated module carries no state, so the single instance is a compile-time type rather than an object, and the schema lives in code, which makes schema/query mismatches compile errors. Choose this variant when the project wants static checking and does not need async.
pitfalls: The table! DSL is per-module: glob-importing users::dsl::* lets short column names collide across tables - import only the columns a function uses.

A multi-statement rule must run inside conn.transaction(|conn| ...); without it each statement commits separately, and the generated schema file must stay in version control because it is code that reviews must see.

variants.name: sqlx async queries over Vec<T>
variants.implementation_notes: sqlx drops the generated module: queries are macros checked against a live database (or against offline query data) and the table module is a set of async functions returning Vec<Row> through fetch_all, so the record set is the vector and there is no table type at all. The trade-off against Diesel is where errors surface: sqlx validates SQL and column types at compile time only when the database is reachable or the offline data is current, while the module stays async-friendly and needs no schema codegen. Choose it when the stack is already async (tokio) and the team prefers SQL in the source.
pitfalls: query! macros need either a live DATABASE_URL at build time or a checked-in .sqlx offline cache; a stale cache lets a renamed column compile and fail at runtime instead.
fetch_all materializes the whole result set without a LIMIT - for large tables stream with fetch and try_next, and remember that pool checkouts are held for the duration of a streamed query.
